newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Kohl says Europe's economy depends on EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kohl says Europe's economy depends on EMU.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Wednesday pinned Europe's economic hopes on the success of monetary union, but opposition leaders said his drive for a hard euro would worsen the continent's jobless crisis.
Kohl, speaking on the second day of parliament's budget debate, told deputies that economic and monetary union (EMU) should go ahead as planned in 1999.
As many of the EU's 15 member nations should join as could meet and stick to the strict Maastricht Treaty conditions for taking part in a single currency.
"We need the euro now, not at some time in the future," he said. "The euro will strengthen the competitiveness of Germany and Europe against the dollar and the yen."
In a reference to mounting calls in France for a franc devaluation, Kohl said any realignment of the European Monetary System's (EMS) currency grid would damage the euro's strength.
"Suggestions to weaken the stability criteria or to devalue a certain currency in the EMS are not compatible with this cause and are harmful for the future," Kohl said.
"We want a hard currency...That is not arrogance, but comes from 50 years of experience in Germany," he said.

Kohl came under attack from Oskar Lafontaine, leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), for trying to enforce a so-called "stability pact" of fiscal discipline which Lafontaine said would boost unemployment.
"With 18 million out of work in Europe we don't need a stability pact, but a pact for jobs and growth," he said.
"We cannot stick to a policy which is creating ever higher unemployment. I am concerned for Franco-German relations."
Prominent Frenchmen like former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing have called for a franc devaluation.
And former European Commission president Jacques Delors said in an open letter to "a German friend" published on Wednesday that the stability pact should also emphasise growth.
With over four million out of work in Germany, Lafontaine said austerity measures in the 1997 budget -- like cuts in job creation schemes -- were ill-timed in a period of slow growth.
The government budget aims to cut the deficit to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product to ensure that Germany fulfils one of the main criteria for entry into monetary union.
The measure should pass easily through the lower house at a final vote on Friday thanks to Kohl's nine-seat majority.
But the SPD, which controls the Bundesrat upper house, has blocked tax changes sought under the 14-year Kohl government's austerity plans -- including the abolition of wealth taxes.
In a stormy debate, Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), slammed the SPD for pursuing an outdated agenda of "redistribution and envy".
A new SPD plan to impose a levy on firms to finance training schemes would destroy jobs, not create them, Schaeuble added.

Lafontaine replied that the government had accepted the outstretched hand of trade unions earlier this year in agreeing an alliance for jobs to halve unemployment by the year 2000 -- only to later cut back welfare benefits like sick pay.
"Has this government lost all its instincts?" he asked.
With government and opposition at loggerheads and two years to go until a general election, Kohl said Germany's voters would have the last word.
"With the blockade you (the SPD) are trying to carry out, you are trying to handicap the government and cash in at the elections in 1998," he said.
"But it won't succeed and you will come away empty-handed."
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-2609750
